This is the author, Mary Pope Osborne.
Chapter one, Way Down Yonder in New Orleans.
He was dreaming that he was sleeping on a boat.
It was rocking back and forth, back and forth… “Jack.”
It was just getting light outside.
Rain was tapping against the window-pane.
Jack opened one eye and looked up.
Annie stood next to his bed.
She was even wearing her raincoat.
Jack turned over and pulled the covers over his head.
It’s really early, and it’s raining.”
They were wearing their cloaks and looking out the tree house window.”
“I just dreamed I was sleeping on a boat.”
“But my dream was real, Jack,” said Annie.
“I guess you want me to go there all by myself.
You want me to have a great adventure while you just lie here, dreaming about sleeping.
If that’s really what you want, I’ll leave you alone.”
“Don’t worry, I will,” said Annie, and she left Jack’s room.
Jack lay still for a moment, listening to the rain fall outside.
Darn, he thought, what if she’s right?
Then he climbed out of bed.
He pulled on his clothes and grabbed his backpack.
He slipped down the stairs, put on his rain boots and raincoat, then headed out the front door.
Annie was standing on the porch, waiting for him.
But as he and Annie took off into the cool, rainy dawn, he woke up completely.
As they charged up the sidewalk, Jack’s heart pounded with excitement.
By the time they headed into the Frog Creek woods, Jack felt like he’d dreamed Annie’s dream, too.
Jack and Annie scrunched over fallen red and gold leaves until they came to the tallest oak.
And Teddy and Kathleen were dressed in their dark cloaks, looking out the window.
Teddy and Kathleen smiled, as if this news didn’t surprise them at all.
Annie and Jack started up the rope ladder.
When they climbed inside the tree house, they hugged the two young enchanters.
“Do you have a new mission for us?”
“Just like last time, Merlin wants you to help a creative person bring his gifts to the world.”
“And this will help you,” said Kathleen.
She pulled a book from her cloak.
He took the book from Kathleen.
The cover showed a street parade with musicians playing trumpets and trombones.
The title was A History of New Orleans Music.
“You will love this city,” said Teddy.
Kathleen picked up a gleaming silver flute from the corner of the tree house.
It was the magic flute Jack had played on their adventure in Vienna, Austria.
“Only this time…” Kathleen tossed the flute into the air.
It hovered for a moment, then began to twirl around and around.
There was a flash of blue light —and the flute was gone!
Floating in its place was a shining brass instrument.
Kathleen plucked the instrument from the air.
“This time you will play a magic trumpet,” she said.
“I’ve always wanted to play the trumpet.”
“Well, this is your chance,” she said.
“The trumpet’s magic will make you a brilliant performer.”
“But the magic can only happen once,” Teddy reminded Jack and Annie, “just as on your last journey with the magic flute.
Play the trumpet only when you face your greatest danger.”
“And while one of us plays, the other has to make up a song, right?”
“And whatever we sing will come true.”
“Um… what danger will we face in New Orleans?”
“But keep the magic trumpet with you just in case.
And remember, after you have played it, the magic will be gone and it will become an ordinary trumpet.”
“Can you tell us what kind of creative genius we’re looking for?”
“We can do more than that,” said Kathleen with a smile.
“He is the King of Jazz,” said Teddy.
“But Louis Armstrong won’t know that when you meet him.
It is your job to put him on the right path.”
“To give his gifts to the world,” said Annie.
He pointed at the cover of the book.
“I wish we could go there,” he said.
said Teddy as he and Kathleen waved good-bye.
The tree house started to spin.
The hot, muggy air was filled with noise.
Jack and Annie heard the clippity-clop of horses’ hooves.
They heard voices calling out “Crawfish pies!”
Jack looked down at his and Annie’s clothes.
They were both wearing white shirts and dark trousers with suspenders.
Jack’s backpack had turned into a cloth bag.
Neither Jack nor Annie was wearing shoes.
“And at least I can run in these pants.
I like them a lot better than the dress I wore on our last mission.”
Jack smiled, remembering Annie’s long, frilly dress in Vienna and his velvet coat and white wig.
“I like being barefoot, too,” he said.
“But what year did we come to?
I can’t tell from our outfits.”
Jack and Annie looked out the window.
The tree house had landed in a grove of palm trees.
Not far away, steamboats churned down a river.
Below them was a bustling city scene.
Rows of stores lined both sides of a wide street.
Vendors were selling food from carts.
Women shoppers wore long skirts, and men wore white suits and hats.
Mule carts and horse-drawn buggies bumped alongside a few antique-looking cars.
Moving down the middle of the street were red and green train cars.
Each one was attached to an electric line overhead.
“This is definitely a long time ago,” said Jack.
“Maybe our research book can help us,” said Jack.
Jack looked in the index of A History of New Orleans Music and found a chapter on Louis Armstrong.
He read: Born in New Orleans in 1901, Louis Armstrong grew up to be one of the greatest jazz musicians who ever lived.
A photo showed an African American man playing a trumpet.
His cheeks were puffed out and his eyes were closed.
Stage lights were shining on him.
Thousands of people were in the audience.
The caption under the photo read Louis Armstrong, King of Jazz.
“It’s a kind of music,” said Jack.
Jack looked up jazz in the glossary of their book.
He read: Jazz began in New Orleans in the early 1900s and was first played by African Americans.
It is a style of music that has a strong beat and is played with lots of feeling.
Jazz melodies are often made up on the spot.
Jack flipped back to the pages about Louis Armstrong and read: As a young teenager, Louis Armstrong often performed with “kid bands” on the streets of the city.
Eventually he played with older musicians in dance halls and developed his musical talents performing on Mississippi riverboats.
When he was twenty-one, he moved to Chicago, where— “Stop.
That’s all we need,” Annie broke in.
“Yep, we’ll just ask someone what the date is,” said Annie.
“Then we can figure out how old Louis Armstrong is, and we’ll know where to look for him: the streets, a dance hall, or on the Mississippi River.”
Annie picked up the magic trumpet.
She tucked it under her arm and started down the rope ladder.
“I guess that’s a plan,” murmured Jack.
He put the New Orleans book in his bag and followed her.
In their bare feet, Jack and Annie hurried a short distance to the wide, busy street.
The sidewalks on both sides of Canal Street were crowded with vendors pushing carts and shouting in rich, loud voices.
Jack and Annie ran over to the boy selling newspapers.
Jack and Annie dug into their pockets.
“Can you just tell us the date?”
“October thirty-first, the eve of All Saints’ Day,” said the boy.
Before Jack could think of an answer, Annie blurted out, “We’re musicians.
We came all the way from Frog Creek, Pennsylvania.”
And it’s a different year in Frog Creek, Pennsylvania, than here in New Orleans, Louisiana!
The newsboy headed up the street, laughing at his own joke.
“Okay, Louis Armstrong was born in 1901, so if it’s 1915…” “He’s fourteen years old,” said Annie.
“So that means he’s playing with kid bands in the streets.
she called to the buttermilk man.
“Can you tell us where some kid bands might be playing today?”
“Try Jackson Square in the French Quarter,” said the man.
“It’s the oldest section of the city,” said the buttermilk man.
“Catch that streetcar that’s stopping up ahead!
It will take you right there.”
She and Jack ran up the sidewalk.
“So I guess those train cars in the street are called streetcars,” said Jack.
Jack and Annie ran to a streetcar stop.
They stood in line and then climbed aboard.
“Hey, sonny, are you coming or going?”
We made a mistake,” said Jack.
It’s the eve of All Saints’ Day,” said the conductor.
He and Annie chose a wooden seat near the door and sat down.
“Could you tell us when to get out for Jackson Square in the French Quarter?”
Annie rested their magic trumpet on her lap.
“Lucky for us we came here on the eve of All Saints’ Day,” she said to Jack.
As the streetcar headed along Canal, he looked up All Saints’ Day in their book.
He read aloud: November first is celebrated as All Saints’ Day in New Orleans.
It is a day to honor those who have passed away.
Sometimes on the eve of All Saints’ Day, people wear costumes and have parties and parades.
Considered the spookiest night of the year, the eve of All Saints’ Day is a good time for ghost sightings.
“The eve of All Saints’ Day sounds like Halloween,” said Annie.
“It’s the same day, too: October thirty-first.”
“But what do they mean, ‘a good time for ghost sightings’?”
He kept reading: The city of New Orleans is often called the most haunted city in America.
According to legend, the old blacksmith shop on Bourbon Street is haunted by the ghost of the famous pirate Jean Lafitte.
Some say that Saint Louis Cathedral is haunted by a Spanish priest, and that a hotel on Chartres Street is haunted by Confederate soldiers.
There have been ghost sightings in many other places throughout the city as well.
We didn’t come to New Orleans to look for ghosts.
We came here to look for Louis Armstrong, the King of Jazz.”
The streetcar turned onto a crowded, busy street.
Lively music blared from restaurants and dance halls.
“We’re in the French Quarter now, and you’re the next stop,” the conductor said to Jack and Annie.
Peter Street toward the Mississippi River.
You’ll run right into Jackson Square.”
Jack put the research book back in his bag.
Annie tucked the trumpet under her arm.
When the streetcar came to a stop, they hopped off.
As the streetcar pulled away, Jack and Annie looked around.
“Hey, this is Bourbon Street,” said Annie, pointing to a street sign.
“Isn’t that the street with the haunted blacksmith shop?”
Jack and Annie left Bourbon Street and started down St.
They passed tall, narrow houses painted pale green, yellow, and pink.
Vines grew up walls and twined around iron balconies.
Alleys led to courtyards with trickling fountains.
“I like the buildings in New Orleans,” said Annie.
“Yeah, and it smells good, too,” said Jack.
Delicious food smells filled the air.
From a muledrawn cart, an old woman cried out, “Waffles!
Outside a restaurant was a sign that read: Special!
“Gosh, things are cheap in 1915,” said Jack.
“Too bad we don’t even have a dime.”
She pointed to a grand cathedral with soaring spires.
That must be the place with the ghost of the Spanish priest.”
“Why do you like ghosts so much?”
“I don’t like ghosts so much,” said Annie.
“Well, you keep talking about them,” said Jack.
“I’m just pointing things out,” said Annie.
“You’re the one who brought up ghosts in the first place.”
He didn’t even like thinking about them.
Soon Jack and Annie came to a huge green park with an iron fence around it.
A sign at the entrance read: JACKSON SQUARE.
Outside the iron fence, in the hot afternoon sunlight, small bands of barefoot kids were playing music.
Others played harmonicas or long tin horns.
A couple of the smallest kids passed around hats, collecting money for the different bands.
“No one here looks like the picture in our book.”
“The picture shows him as a grown-up.
He wouldn’t look the same when he’s fourteen.”
She went up to a small girl passing a hat.
“Excuse me, is there a musician here named Louis Armstrong?”
the girl shouted to the biggest kid in the singing trio.
“Just saw him—he’s at the River Café!”
He's at the River Cafe, shouted little Mac.
“Down by the river,” said the small girl.
“Walk down Decatur Street and you’ll see it.”
The girl held up the hat, as if asking for a donation.
“But thanks for your help,” said Annie.
She and Jack left the square.
“So Dipper must be a nickname for Louis Armstrong,” said Jack.
“And Dipper must be playing music at the café.”
He pointed to a red sign on a slanted rooftop.
Jack and Annie walked under a striped red awning.
Waiters in white jackets were running around with trays of coffee and delicious-smelling doughnuts.
There’s no music here,” said Annie.
“Excuse us,” she called to one of the waiters.
Or Dip—” “Did you come here to buy something, kids?”
“No, we don’t have any money—” started Jack.
“We’re looking for —” “I know beggars when I see them!
I don’t think Dipper’s in here, anyway,” said Jack.
“Wait a minute, I have to tell them that we’re not beggars!”
“It’s not worth it, come on,” said Jack.
Jack was mad, too, but he pulled Annie out from under the awning.
“I think it’s the way we look,” he said.
And we don’t have shoes on.”
We’ll ask someone else where to find Dipper,” said Jack.
On the street by the café was a mule cart filled with coal.
A young teenager was putting a bucket and shovel into the back of the cart.
He was barefoot and wore clothes like Jack and Annie’s.
When he saw Jack and Annie, he grinned.
He had the friendliest smile Jack had ever seen.
How can I help you, man?”
Jack was at a loss for words.
He hadn’t thought about what to say to Louis Armstrong when they found him.
said Annie, walking up to the boy.
“We’re Jack and Annie from Frog Creek, Pennsylvania.
Friends of ours told us to find you when we came to New Orleans.”
But then his gaze fell on Annie’s trumpet.
“Only when the time is right,” said Annie.
“I won’t know till I feel it,” said Annie.
Dipper smiled his radiant smile again.
I know just what you mean!”
He wiped his hand on his pants and held it out to shake.
“Any friends of Teddy and Kathleen’s are friends of mine.”
As Jack shook Dipper’s hand, he sputtered, “You— you know Teddy and Kathleen?”
“No, man, never heard of them,” said Dipper.
“Only problem is I can’t hang out with y’all right now,” said Dipper.
He climbed onto the mule cart.
“I’m making my rounds with this coal cart,” said Dipper.
“And I have lots more work to do today.
But be sure to look me up the next time you come to town.
And say hi to my pals, Teddy and Kathleen.”
Dipper waved at them and then shook the reins.
The mule clopped over the brick street, pulling the coal cart away from the River Café.
“We have to follow him,” said Annie.
“We can’t let him out of our sight.”
Jack and Annie walked quickly after the mule cart.
The hot brick road burned their feet.
“So let’s figure out—ow—what we’re going to say to him,” said Jack.
“We’ll tell him we’d like to work with him.
And then while we’re working, we’ll start talking to him about music.
And put him on the right path to becoming the King of Jazz.”
It wasn’t much of a plan, but he couldn’t think of anything better.
Up ahead, Dipper’s mule cart stopped near the back of a candy shop.
Y’all are sticking to me like glue,” he said.
“Well, actually, we were wondering—” started Jack.
We think it might be fun,” said Annie.
We just like to work,” said Annie.
“Yeah, yeah, we really do,” said Jack.
I reckon there’s enough work to go around today,” he said.
“There’s extra shovels and buckets in the cart.”
Just tell us what to do, Dipper,” said Annie.
“Fill your buckets with coal and toss each bucket load into the bin,” said Dipper.
He pointed to a large wooden box at the back of the small candy shop.
Annie carefully set the magic trumpet on the ground near Dipper’s cart.
Jack left his cloth bag beside it.
Dipper handed each of them a heavy shovel and a tin bucket from the back of the cart.
Then all three of them started shoveling coal.
But Jack and Annie had a hard time handling their heavy shovels.
Whenever the shovels tipped to the side, all the coal fell off.
Finally they both just grabbed pieces of coal with their hands and tossed them into their buckets.
The afternoon sun beat down on Jack’s back as he worked.
He was sweaty and short of breath.
His hands were black from picking up the coal, and his clothes were covered with coal dust.
This is a terrible job, he thought.
He wondered how Dipper could be so cheerful.
“So, Dipper,” said Annie, “do you like music?”
Dipper’s answer was drowned out as he dumped a load of coal into the bin.
Dipper answered again, but Jack didn’t hear him because a buggy rumbled by.
This is a bad time for a serious discussion, Jack thought.
He could hardly think in the burning sun.
As Dipper shoveled more coal, he started singing a song that seemed to give words to how Jack felt: I’ve got those coal cart blues.
I’m really all confused— I’m about to lose my very mind.
But Dipper didn’t seem confused at all, or about to lose his mind.
He had a warm, raspy voice, and his song had a lively beat.
Three boys were running toward the coal cart.
They were the singing trio Jack and Annie had seen on Jackson Square.
“I know you’re working,” said one of the kids.
We just got a gig to sing in the parade.”
“Sorry, can’t do it, Little Mack,” said Dipper.
Little Mack wasn’t exactly little, Jack noticed.
He looked like he weighed over two hundred pounds.
He didn’t look happy at all.
“Can’t do it, Big Nose,” said Dipper.
Jack looked at Big Nose’s nose.
Y’all sound just fine by yourselves,” said Dipper.
“Go on to the parade and have fun.”
“Since sunup, I’ve delivered five cartloads of coal.
I get paid fifteen cents a load.
That makes seventy-five cents I’m going to take home to my family tonight.
How much did you fellas make on the square today?
How much you going to make in the parade?”
“I’ve got a steady job now,” said Dipper.
Go on to the parade and have a good time.”
The three boys stared at Dipper for a long moment.
“Come on, fellas,” Little Mack said finally.
Ever since he got back from the Waif’s Home, he’s turned into a mama’s boy.”
Jack wondered what the Waif’s Home was.
Dipper watched the three boys walk off.
Then he looked at Jack and Annie.
“Little Mack, Happy, and Big Nose Sidney are old buddies of mine,” he explained with a sigh.
“Dipper, can’t you take just a little time off and go with your buddies to sing in the parade?”
“That’s just the way it has to be.”
Dipper went back to shoveling coal.
Jack wanted to ask him about the Waif’s Home, but Dipper didn’t look like he wanted to talk.
He didn’t sing anymore as he filled up his coal bucket.
If Dipper doesn’t perform, he’ll never grow up to be the King of Jazz, Jack thought.
He’ll never give his gifts to the world.
“Dipper, do you have to support your family all by yourself?
You’re pretty young for that, aren’t you?”
“Mama Lucy, Mayann, and baby Clarence are all depending on me.”
“Yep, and I love them a lot,” said Dipper.
“But what about giving your gifts to the world?”
“I can’t afford gifts for Lady the mule.
How am I going to afford gifts for the world?”
I’ll sing a song to Lady on her birthday,” he said.
Dipper tossed his shovel into the bucket.
Then he reached into his pocket and took out some change.
“Tomorrow I’ll be getting paid fifteen cents for this load,” he said.
“In case I don’t see you again, here’s your share: five cents for you and five for you.”
“You should keep it all for your family, Dipper.”
“Then what did y’all do that work for?”
“We didn’t do that much,” Jack said.
“Not nearly as much as you did.
It was a lot harder job than I thought it would be.”
“It was fun hanging out with you,” said Annie.
“Well, you two sure are a couple of potato heads,” he said.
“It means you don’t have any more brains than a pair of potatoes,” said Dipper.
“Well, thanks a million for your help,” said Dipper.
He climbed back into the driver’s seat of the cart.
“Hey want me and Lady to give y’all a ride back to the coal yard?”
Jack grabbed his bag, and they sat on the cart bench next to Dipper.
Jack was still hot and sweaty.
He was tired and his arms were sore.
But for some reason, he felt great.
Lady the mule began pulling the creaky cart along the Mississippi River.
And Dipper began singing again: I’ve got those coal cart blues.
I’m really all confused… The sky had grown cloudy, and a warm breeze was blowing.
Dipper stopped the cart and listened.
Jack heard band music in the distance.
“Is that parade for All Saints’ Day?”
Or maybe for a million other things,” said Dipper.
“Folks in this city will find any excuse for a parade.”
Soon the parade came into view.
Horseback riders wore plumed hats and black masks.
Following them were people dressed up as clowns, kings, queens, fairies with fluttering wings, ghosts, and skeletons.
“We read that New Orleans might be the most haunted city in the country,” Annie said to Dipper, “especially on the eve of All Saints’ Day.
We heard there’re real ghosts in a cathedral, a hotel, and a blacksmith shop.”
“Yeah, and plenty more places, too,” said Dipper.
A band followed the people in costumes.
The musicians were playing trumpets, tubas, trombones, and drums—lots of drums.
The joyous music filled the New Orleans air.
Jack and Annie couldn’t help nodding their heads in time to the beat.
Jack noticed that Dipper was nodding his head, too.
Happy, Little Mack, and Big Nose Sidney were walking alongside the band, singing their hearts out.
I wish I had musical talent!
“Musical talent is really a great gift to share with the world!”
Dipper just shook his head, as if he thought they were crazy.
“Biggest potato heads I’ve ever met,” he said.
Dipper gave the reins a shake.
How weird that Dipper said that, Jack thought.
Their mission was to keep him on the right path, too—the path to becoming the King of Jazz.
As Lady plodded along the bank of the Mississippi, Dipper started singing nonsense words: Skid-dat-de-dat Skid-dat-de-doo!
I’m just scat-singing, man,” said Dipper.
“When you can’t think of words, just sing sounds,” said Dipper.
If you put your heart in it, folks will understand you.”
“I didn’t know a person could make music like that,” said Jack.
“Heck, yeah, you can make music any way you want,” said Dipper.
“Just listen to the world: There’s church bells, the washerwoman singing about her wash, the ragman blasting his tin horn for folks to bring out their rags.
Folks selling things, like that pie man.
Dipper pointed to a man sitting in a red wagon, calling out in a strong, rich voice, “Sweet potato!

The women carried baskets on their heads and called out in singsong voices, “Blue-berries!”
“I see what you mean,” said Annie.
“You can even hear it in Lady’s hoofbeats.
You can even hear it in ladies hoof beats.
Jack listened to the rhythmic clippity-clop, clippityclop of the mule.
“That’s a song— Go ’long, mule, go ’long, mule.”
Jack and Annie listened to the steady music of Lady’s hoofbeats, until finally the mule came to a stop.
“Well, here we are at the coal yard,” said Dipper.
They all jumped to the ground.
Dipper patted the mule on her nose.
Then he turned to Jack and Annie.
“Afraid I have to leave y’all now,” Dipper said.
“Yeah, um…,” Jack began, trying to think of a good reason to stay with Dipper.
“I’d like to hear you blow that horn when the time’s right,” Dipper said to Annie.
“And don’t forget to say hi to Teddy and Kathleen for me.”
He winked, then waved and started walking away.
He waved again and kept going.
Jack and Annie looked at each other in a panic.
She and Jack ran after him.
“I have to haul bananas till dark.”
Dipper stopped and stared at them.
“Don’t you know how to have fun?”
Jack didn’t know what to say.
And you make everything more fun with your singing.”
“Remember when I said you didn’t have any more brains than a pair of potatoes?
I don’t think you have one potato’s brain between you.”
Jack and Annie hurried with Dipper down to the loading dock on the riverfront.
At least fifty workers were hauling huge loads of bananas out of the cargo hold of a ship.
Dipper walked over to a man checking people in to work.
He pointed to Jack and Annie.
Dipper waved for them to come join him.
Jack and Annie ran down to join Dipper and the other workers in the cargo hold.
Dipper picked up a giant bunch of bananas.
The bunch was almost as big as Annie!
He hauled it onto his shoulder and then picked up another one.
“Grab a bunch of bananas and follow me!”
He headed to the counter, where men in white suits were inspecting the banana bunches.
“No way either of us can pick up one of those bunches,” Jack said to Annie.
Annie hid their trumpet behind a large wooden box.
Jack put his bag there, too.
Jack and Annie loaded a bunch of bananas into their arms.
They walked closely together, taking short, clumsy steps, following Dipper.
They delivered the bunch to the inspectors and then hurried back to get another.
As the sun sank toward the river, Jack, Annie, and Dipper hauled bananas back and forth between the cargo hold and the inspectors.
They hauled bananas until it was almost dark.
Jack was so tired he could hardly see straight.
He was afraid Dipper would never call it quits.
Suddenly a large rat jumped out of the cargo hold!
He dropped his bananas and took off running.
Annie and Jack dropped their bananas, too.
Jack grabbed his bag, and they ran after Dipper.
Running like crazy, Dipper led Jack and Annie far from the loading area—and the rat.
When he finally stopped, Jack bumped into Dipper, and Annie bumped into Jack.
He collapsed on the curb of Decatur Street and laughed so hard his whole body shook.
Jack and Annie sat down next to him, laughing until they cried.
Finally they all managed to calm down.
“I know… I know I said I wasn’t afraid of anything,” Dipper said breathlessly.
I’m afraid of one thing: rats.
“Yeah, yeah,” Annie said, catching her breath.
“That’s cool, that’s cool, man,” said Dipper.
“Between the three of us, we got all the scaredy stuff covered.”
That made them all start laughing again.
As the twilight deepened, they sat on the curb, catching their breath.
They laughed now and then, out of relief and friendship.
“Before we part ways, I better get our pay from the boss.
Jack and Annie kept sitting on the curb as Dipper ran back down to the dock.
We can’t part ways yet,” said Jack.

a man shouted as he walked by.

Big storm comin’ for the eve of All Saints’!”

He and Annie jumped up from the curb and bounded off with Dipper.
Chapter six, find me at the greasy spoon.
Streetlamps were coming on as Jack, Annie, and Dipper walked away from Jackson Square.
When they came to Bourbon Street, vendors walked the sidewalks, calling out, “Ice cream!”
“There seems to be lots of good food in New Orleans.”
People were sitting outside dance halls and restaurants, laughing and talking, eating and drinking.
Outside and inside, musicians were blaring away on their instruments.
Hey, there's Dipper, seeing something for us, Dipper?
“Hey, girl, can you play that trumpet?”
“She’ll know it when she feels it!”

Dipper led Jack and Annie down a narrow alley to the back of a shabby, run-down building.

He was carrying a big bowl and a tall glass.
“I got us some gumbo stew and some lemonade to share!”
Dipper sat between Jack and Annie on the steps.
He pulled spoons out of his pocket for each of them.
Together the three of them tackled the gumbo stew.
They all ate their fill of spicy chicken, ham, tomatoes, okra, onions, and rice.
